paragraphs.heading: Places built for watching
paragraphs.text: An observatory is a place for observing events on land, at sea or in the sky. Observatories have been built for astronomy, climate and weather science, geophysics, oceanography and volcanology, though some people still keep the word for astronomy alone. Astronomical observatories are mainly sorted by location: in space, in the air, on the ground or underground. They can be private or public.

paragraphs.heading: On the ground
paragraphs.text: Early ground-based observatories could be as simple as a mural instrument, used to measure angles between stars, or Stonehenge, which has some alignments with astronomical events. Observatories on Earth's surface make observations in the radio and visible light parts of the spectrum. Most optical telescopes sit inside a dome that protects their delicate instruments from the elements. The dome has a slit that opens during observing, and in most cases its whole upper part rotates so the telescope can see different parts of the sky. Radio telescopes usually have no dome.

paragraphs.heading: Picking a site
paragraphs.text: Most optical observatories on the ground sit far from big cities to escape light pollution. The best sites have dark skies, many clear nights a year, dry air and high elevation. Up high the air is thinner, which reduces turbulence and gives better astronomical "seeing". Good places include the southwestern United States, Hawaii, the Canary Islands, the Andes and high Mexican mountains such as Sierra Negra. Major optical observatories include Mauna Kea and Kitt Peak in the US, Roque de los Muchachos in Spain, and Paranal and Cerro Tololo in Chile.

paragraphs.heading: Higher and higher
paragraphs.text: A 2009 study found that the best spot on Earth for a ground observatory is Ridge A in central East Antarctica, with the least atmospheric disturbance and the best visibility. Since the mid-20th century, several observatories have been built above 4,000–5,000 metres. The largest is Mauna Kea, near the top of a 4,205-metre volcano in Hawaiʻi. Bolivia's Chacaltaya observatory, at 5,230 m, was the highest permanent astronomical observatory from the 1940s until 2009. It has since been overtaken by the University of Tokyo Atacama Observatory, on a 5,640 m peak in Chile's Atacama Desert.

paragraphs.heading: Radio observatories
paragraphs.text: Since 1933, radio telescopes have been built to study the universe in the radio part of the spectrum. A radio observatory is one or more such instruments plus support facilities, such as control centres, visitor housing and maintenance buildings. These also sit far from cities, to avoid interference from radio, TV and radar, but unlike optical sites they can be placed in valleys for extra shielding. Major examples include the Very Large Array in New Mexico, Arecibo in Puerto Rico, Jodrell Bank in the UK, Chajnantor in Chile and Parkes in Australia.

paragraphs.heading: Above the air
paragraphs.text: Space-based observatories are telescopes or other instruments in outer space, many of them orbiting Earth. The atmosphere blocks ultraviolet light, X-rays and gamma rays and partly blocks infrared, so these are best observed from above it. Space telescopes also escape the turbulence that troubles ground-based views, so one like Hubble often has a much smaller angular resolution than a ground telescope of similar aperture. The price is steep: they cost far more to build and are very hard to maintain. Hubble could be serviced by the Space Shuttles, but many other space telescopes cannot be.

paragraphs.heading: Planes and balloons
paragraphs.text: Airborne observatories have the advantage of height, putting them above most of the atmosphere. Compared with space telescopes, their instruments can be deployed, repaired and updated much faster and more cheaply. Two examples, the Stratospheric Observatory for Infrared Astronomy and the Kuiper Airborne Observatory, use airplanes to observe in the infrared, which water vapour in the air absorbs. Many countries have also flown high-altitude balloons for X-ray astronomy.
